      <title>Node Selectors and Node Affinity: Telling the Scheduler Where Pods Can Run</title>
      <dc:creator>Siddharth More</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 06:25:26 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/siddharthajmore/node-selectors-and-node-affinity-telling-the-scheduler-where-pods-can-run-1loj</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/siddharthajmore/node-selectors-and-node-affinity-telling-the-scheduler-where-pods-can-run-1loj</guid>
      <description><p><strong>TL;DR</strong></p>

<ul>
<li>
<code>nodeSelector</code> matches a pod to a node using labels. Simple, exact match, nothing fancier.</li>
<li>Node affinity does the same job with more expressive rules: <code>In</code>, <code>NotIn</code>, <code>Exists</code>, <code>DoesNotExist</code>, <code>Gt</code>, <code>Lt</code>.</li>
<li>Affinity comes in two flavors: <code>required</code> (hard rule) and <code>preferred</code> (soft nudge, weighted).</li>
<li>
<code>IgnoredDuringExecution</code> means once the pod's running, changes to the node's labels don't affect it. No eviction, no re-check.</li>
</ul>

<p>Skip around if you already know the basics:</p>

<ul>
<li>The problem this actually solves</li>
<li>nodeSelector vs node affinity, explained</li>
<li>Where node selection actually matters</li>
<li>What the scheduler's doing under the hood</li>
<li>nodeSelector vs affinity, the trade-offs</li>
<li>What goes wrong, and why</li>
<li>Try it yourself</li>
</ul>

<h2>
  
  
  WHY: the problem
</h2>

<p>In Part 1, we saw kube-scheduler filter out nodes that can't run a pod, then score whatever's left. That's default. Most of the time, you don't need to touch it.</p>

<p>But sometimes the scheduler doesn't know something you know. Maybe only some of your nodes have GPUs. Maybe a database needs SSD-backed storage, and a spinning disk will tank its performance. Nothing in a plain pod spec tells the scheduler to care about that.</p>

<p>Node selectors and node affinity exist to close that gap. They let you attach the missing context yourself.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  WHAT: the two mechanisms
</h2>

<p>Both work off the same idea: label your nodes, then tell the pod which labels to look for.</p>

<p><strong><code>nodeSelector</code></strong> is the simple version. Give it one or more key-value pairs, and the pod only lands on a node that has every one of them.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">apiVersion</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">v1</span>
<span class="na">kind</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">Pod</span>
<span class="na">metadata</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">name</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">nodeselector-pod</span>
<span class="na">spec</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">nodeSelector</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">disktype</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">ssd</span>
  <span class="na">containers</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">name</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">nginx</span>
    <span class="na">image</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">nginx</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p><strong>Node affinity</strong> does the same job, but with real operators instead of one flat match: <code>In</code>, <code>NotIn</code>, <code>Exists</code>, <code>DoesNotExist</code>, <code>Gt</code>, <code>Lt</code>. </p>

<blockquote>
<p>Worth noting: there's no separate "node anti-affinity" field - using NotIn or DoesNotExist as the operator is what gets you that behavior, keeping a pod away from nodes that match instead of drawing it toward them.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>It also splits into two types:</p>

<ul>
<li>
<code>requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution</code> - a hard rule, functionally like <code>nodeSelector</code> but more expressive</li>
<li>
<code>preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution</code> - a soft rule with a weight (1-100) that nudges the scheduler's scoring, without blocking the pod if nothing matches
</li>
</ul>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">apiVersion</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">v1</span>
<span class="na">kind</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">Pod</span>
<span class="na">metadata</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">name</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">affinity-pod</span>
<span class="na">spec</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">affinity</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">nodeAffinity</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="na">requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution</span><span class="pi">:</span>
        <span class="na">nodeSelectorTerms</span><span class="pi">:</span>
        <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
          <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">key</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">disktype</span>
            <span class="na">operator</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">In</span>
            <span class="na">values</span><span class="pi">:</span>
            <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s">hdd</span>
      <span class="na">preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">weight</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="m">50</span>
        <span class="na">preference</span><span class="pi">:</span>
          <span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
          <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">key</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">zone</span>
            <span class="na">operator</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">In</span>
            <span class="na">values</span><span class="pi">:</span>
            <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s">us-east-1a</span>
  <span class="na">containers</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">name</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">nginx</span>
    <span class="na">image</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">nginx</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Read that as: this pod <strong>MUST</strong> land on an HDD node, and it would prefer <code>us-east-1a</code>, but it won't sit <code>Pending</code> for the zone to match.</p>

<p>One thing that trips people up: <code>nodeSelectorTerms</code> doesn't just take <code>matchExpressions</code>. It also takes <code>matchFields</code>, and the two aren't interchangeable.</p>

<p><code>matchExpressions</code> matches against node <strong>labels</strong>, the same labels you set earlier. <code>matchFields</code> matches against node <strong>fields</strong> instead, things like the node's actual name in the API, not something someone labeled.</p>

<p><code>matchFields</code> lets node affinity match against supported node fields rather than labels. A common example is matching <code>metadata.name</code> to target a particular node.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">apiVersion</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">v1</span>
<span class="na">kind</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">Pod</span>
<span class="na">metadata</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">name</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">pinned-to-node-1</span>
<span class="na">spec</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">affinity</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">nodeAffinity</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="na">requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution</span><span class="pi">:</span>
        <span class="na">nodeSelectorTerms</span><span class="pi">:</span>
        <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">matchFields</span><span class="pi">:</span>
          <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">key</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">metadata.name</span>
            <span class="na">operator</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">In</span>
            <span class="na">values</span><span class="pi">:</span>
            <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s">node-1</span>
  <span class="na">containers</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">name</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">nginx</span>
    <span class="na">image</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">nginx</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Worth being honest about this one: it's rarely the right call. Hard-coding a node name defeats the whole point of a label-based system, and if that node ever gets replaced, your pod just stops scheduling. Reach for <code>matchExpressions</code> and labels first.</p>

<p>There's one more thing worth nailing down: how multiple expressions and values actually combine. It's not obvious just from looking at the YAML.</p>

<p>Inside one <code>matchExpressions</code> list, every entry has to match. That's an AND.</p>

<p>Inside one expression's <code>values</code> list, matching any single value is enough. That's an OR.</p>

<p>And across separate entries in <code>nodeSelectorTerms</code> itself, only one term has to fully match. That's another OR, one level up.</p>

<p>Stacked together, it looks like this:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">spec</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">affinity</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">nodeAffinity</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="na">requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution</span><span class="pi">:</span>
        <span class="na">nodeSelectorTerms</span><span class="pi">:</span>
        <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
          <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">key</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">zone</span>
            <span class="na">operator</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">In</span>
            <span class="na">values</span><span class="pi">:</span>
            <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s">us-east-1a</span>
            <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s">us-east-1b</span>
          <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">key</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">disktype</span>
            <span class="na">operator</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">In</span>
            <span class="na">values</span><span class="pi">:</span>
            <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s">ssd</span>
        <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
          <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">key</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">zone</span>
            <span class="na">operator</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">In</span>
            <span class="na">values</span><span class="pi">:</span>
            <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s">us-west-2a</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Read that as:<br>
<strong>(</strong>zone is (<code>us-east-1a</code> <strong>OR</strong> <code>us-east-1b</code>), <strong>AND</strong> disktype is <code>ssd</code><strong>) <br>
OR <br>
(</strong>zone is <code>us-west-2a</code><strong>)</strong>.</p>

<p>It looks like a lot stacked up like that, but it's really just three separate rules, each with its own logic, nested inside each other.</p>

<blockquote>
<p>You can also use both nodeSelector and nodeAffinity,in that case a node must satisfy both before the Pod can be scheduled.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>📖 Docs: <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#nodeselector" rel="noopener noreferrer">nodeSelector</a> · <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#node-affinity" rel="noopener noreferrer">node affinity</a></p>
<h2>
  
  
  WHEN: where node selection actually matters
</h2>

<p>A few real situations where controlling Pod placement makes sense, regardless of which mechanism you reach for:</p>

<ul>
<li>GPU workloads that should only run on GPU-equipped nodes</li>
<li>Databases or caches that need SSD-backed storage</li>
<li>Workloads you want kept in a specific zone, without hard-blocking if that zone's full</li>
<li>Compliance or licensing rules that pin certain workloads to certain hardware</li>
</ul>

<p>If none of that applies, the scheduler's default behavior is usually fine on its own.</p>
<h2>
  
  
  HOW: what's actually happening
</h2>

<p><code>nodeSelector</code> and the required affinity rule both get evaluated during the filtering phase from Part 1. Any node that doesn't match gets thrown out before scoring even starts.</p>

<p>The preferred affinity rule works differently. It doesn't touch filtering at all. Once the feasible set is decided, the scheduler adds the rule's weight to a node's score if that node matches. Highest score wins, same as any other scoring factor.</p>

<p>Both mechanisms share one behavior worth calling out: they're <em>ignored during execution</em>. The rule only gets checked once, at scheduling time. If someone relabels the node an hour later, nothing happens to the pod already running there.</p>
<h2>
  
  
  TRADE-OFFS: nodeSelector vs affinity
</h2>

<p><code>nodeSelector</code> is less YAML and easier to read. If the requirement really is "must have this one label," there's no reason to reach for affinity instead.</p>

<p>The moment you need OR logic, negation, or a "prefer but don't require," <code>nodeSelector</code> can't do it and affinity can. That flexibility costs a bit more nesting, but there's no real downside beyond that.</p>

<p>One thing neither of these solves: pod-to-pod placement, like "run this next to that" or "spread these apart." That's pod affinity and anti-affinity, coming in Part 4. And if the goal is nodes actively rejecting pods rather than pods choosing nodes, that's taints and tolerations, next up in Part 3.</p>
<h2>
  
  
  FAILURE: what goes wrong
</h2>

<p>The most common failure: you set a required rule, no node matches it, and the pod remains <code>Pending</code> until a suitable node becomes available or the scheduling constraints change. There's no obvious error, just a pod that never starts. <code>kubectl describe pod</code>, specifically its Events section, is where you'll actually see the scheduling failure reason.</p>

<p>The second one catches people off guard: because these rules are <code>IgnoredDuringExecution</code>, relabeling a node does nothing to pods already scheduled there. If you're expecting a label change to trigger a reschedule, it won't. You'd have to delete and recreate the pod yourself.</p>
<h2>
  
  
  PRACTICE: label, deploy, check
</h2>

<p>Label two nodes differently:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl label node node-1 <span class="nv">disktype</span><span class="o">=</span>ssd
kubectl label node node-2 <span class="nv">disktype</span><span class="o">=</span>hdd
kubectl get nodes <span class="nt">--show-labels</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Save the two pod specs from the WHAT section as <code>nodeselector-pod.yaml</code> and <code>affinity-pod.yaml</code>, then deploy both:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl apply <span class="nt">-f</span> nodeselector-pod.yaml
kubectl apply <span class="nt">-f</span> affinity-pod.yaml
kubectl get pods <span class="nt">-o</span> wide
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>For the <code>nodeSelector</code> pod, <code>describe</code> shows it directly:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl describe pod nodeselector-pod
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Look for a <code>Node-Selectors:</code> line. It'll show <code>disktype=ssd</code>.</p>

<p><code>kubectl describe pod</code> is useful for inspecting scheduling information and events, but it isn't the best way to inspect the complete affinity configuration. To see the exact affinity rules attached to the Pod, inspect the Pod spec directly:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl get pod affinity-pod <span class="nt">-o</span> yaml | <span class="nb">grep</span> <span class="nt">-A</span> 16 affinity
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>That's the only reliable way to confirm what's actually attached to a running pod.</p>

<p>Next up, Part 3: taints and tolerations, where instead of pods choosing nodes, nodes start rejecting pods.</p>

<p>For those who read till end, I appreciate your patience since this was bit complex, and I too had to struggle to shape this article.  </p>

<p>If anything here didn't land, or you'd explain it differently, drop a comment. Doubts and pushback are both welcome.</p>

</description>

      <title>Kubernetes 1.30 Adds AI Autoscaling, Elevates Cloud Native Ops</title>
      <dc:creator>TechPulse </dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Wed, 16 Sep 2026 22:38:49 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/techpulse01239/kubernetes-130-adds-ai-autoscaling-elevates-cloud-native-ops-1pbc</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/techpulse01239/kubernetes-130-adds-ai-autoscaling-elevates-cloud-native-ops-1pbc</guid>
      <description><h1>
  
  
  Kubernetes 1.30 Adds AI Autoscaling, Elevates Cloud Native Ops
</h1>

<p><strong>Meta description:</strong> The CNCF releases Kubernetes 1.30 on Aug 14, 2026, introducing AI‑driven autoscaling, enhanced security, and a new LTS roadmap, signaling a major shift for cloud‑native workloads.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  Lead
</h2>

<p>The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) announced the general availability of Kubernetes 1.30 on <strong>August 14, 2026</strong>. The release packs AI‑driven autoscaling, a hardened security model, and a long‑term support (LTS) schedule that promises stability for enterprise workloads. With more than <strong>5,000 contributors</strong> and over <strong>30 %</strong> improvement in resource efficiency, the milestone marks the biggest upgrade in the platform’s history.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  Release Overview
</h2>

<p>Kubernetes 1.30 is the 30th major version of the open‑source container orchestration system that powers the majority of cloud‑native applications today. The CNCF reported <strong>12 new APIs</strong>, <strong>4 beta features</strong>, and <strong>over 1,200 pull requests</strong> merged since the 1.29 release. The version also introduces a <strong>new LTS track</strong>, guaranteeing three years of security patches and bug‑fix updates for customers who need long‑term stability.</p>

<blockquote>
<p>"Kubernetes has always been about empowering developers to ship faster. With AI‑autoscaling, we’re giving them a smarter, self‑optimizing control plane," said <strong>Kelsey Hightower</strong>, Distinguished Engineer at Google and longtime Kubernetes advocate.</p>
</blockquote>

<h2>
  
  
  Key Features
</h2>

<h3>
  
  
  AI‑Driven Autoscaling
</h3>

<p>The standout feature is <strong>AI‑autoscaler</strong>, a machine‑learning controller that predicts workload demand based on historical metrics and scales pods pre‑emptively. Early benchmarks from the CNCF show a <strong>30 % reduction in over‑provisioned resources</strong> and a <strong>15 % improvement in latency</strong> for bursty traffic patterns.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Enhanced Security
</h3>

<p>Version 1.30 adds <strong>Zero‑Trust networking policies</strong>, integrated <strong>SPIFFE</strong> identity verification, and a <strong>runtime security module</strong> that blocks unauthorized system calls. The new policies are backwards‑compatible, allowing clusters to adopt them incrementally.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Improved Observability
</h3>

<p>A revamped <strong>Metrics Server</strong> now supports <strong>Prometheus v3</strong> out‑of‑the‑box, and the <strong>kubectl</strong> CLI includes a <strong>visual diff</strong> mode for easier comparison of manifests across environments.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Why It Matters
</h2>

<p>Kubernetes has become the de‑facto standard for container orchestration, but scaling efficiency and security remain pain points for large enterprises. By embedding AI directly into the control plane, 1.30 reduces the operational overhead that traditionally required custom scripts or third‑party tools. The LTS roadmap also addresses a long‑standing demand from Fortune 500 companies that need predictable upgrade cycles.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Industry Impact
</h2>

<p>The release is already prompting a wave of announcements from cloud providers. <strong>Amazon Web Services (AWS)</strong> said it will enable AI‑autoscaling as a managed feature in <strong>EKS</strong> by Q4 2026, while <strong>Microsoft Azure</strong> plans to integrate the new security policies into <strong>AKS</strong> next month. Startups in the observability space, such as <strong>Chronosphere</strong> and <strong>Grafana Labs</strong>, are updating their integrations to surface AI‑autoscaler metrics, positioning themselves as complementary tools for the new ecosystem.</p>

<p>Analysts at <strong>Gartner</strong> predict that AI‑enhanced orchestration could accelerate cloud‑native adoption by <strong>12 %</strong> in the next two years, especially among regulated industries that value the LTS guarantees.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  What's Next
</h2>

<p>The CNCF has outlined a roadmap that includes <strong>Kubernetes 1.31</strong>, slated for early 2027, which will focus on <strong>edge‑native extensions</strong> and deeper <strong>multi‑cluster federation</strong>. Meanwhile, the community is preparing a <strong>sandbox</strong> for developers to experiment with custom AI models that can be plugged into the autoscaler pipeline.</p>

<p>As the platform continues to mature, the combination of AI, security, and long‑term support positions Kubernetes 1.30 as a pivotal step toward more autonomous, resilient cloud infrastructures.</p>

</description>

      <title>How I Cleared AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner and What I Learned</title>
      <dc:creator>Huzaifa Bin Tariq</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Wed, 16 Sep 2026 04:55:04 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/huzaifa_1302/how-i-cleared-aws-cloud-quest-cloud-practitioner-and-what-i-learned-87p</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/huzaifa_1302/how-i-cleared-aws-cloud-quest-cloud-practitioner-and-what-i-learned-87p</guid>
      <description><p>I recently completed AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner, and honestly, it was one of the most enjoyable ways I have learned cloud computing so far.</p>

<p>What made it different for me was the gamified learning experience. Instead of only watching lectures and taking quizzes, I was solving challenges, building cloud solutions, completing assignments, and moving through a virtual environment.</p>

<p>It actually felt more like playing a game while learning cloud concepts.</p>

<p><strong>What I Learned</strong></p>

<p>During the quest, I completed hands-on challenges covering different areas of AWS, including:</p>

<ul>
<li>Cloud Computing Essentials</li>
<li>Cloud First Steps</li>
<li>Computing Solutions</li>
<li>Networking Concepts</li>
<li>Cloud Economics</li>
<li>Databases in Practice</li>
<li>Connecting VPCs</li>
<li>First NoSQL Database</li>
<li>File Systems in the Cloud</li>
<li>Core Security Concepts</li>
<li>Auto-Healing and Scaling Applications</li>
<li>Highly Available Web Applications</li>
</ul>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F1xffgkdyua3zmmdlguft.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F1xffgkdyua3zmmdlguft.png" alt="Certificate" width="800" height="580"></a></p>

<p>One thing that really stood out to me was how many different parts are involved in building a reliable cloud application.</p>

<p>For example, creating an EC2 instance or an S3 bucket is only one part of the process. Security is also very important. You need to understand who can access your resources, what permissions they have, and how to protect your cloud environment.</p>

<p>Learning about IAM, networking, security, and best practices helped me understand that in the cloud, simply making something work is not enough. It also needs to be secure, reliable, and properly managed.</p>

<p>I also enjoyed learning about cloud economics. Before this, I mostly thought of cloud computing as using online servers and services. But the quest showed me that choosing the right resources and understanding how they are used can have a big impact on cost.</p>

<p>Things like avoiding unnecessary resources, choosing the right services, and scaling based on demand are important when working with cloud platforms.</p>

      <title>Amazon Athena: Querying S3 Data Using SQL | A Hands-on AWS Guide</title>
      <dc:creator>AKSHARANETHRA NP</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Tue, 15 Sep 2026 16:41:53 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/aksharanethra_np_e411e388/amazon-athena-querying-s3-data-using-sql-a-hands-on-aws-guide-32i0</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/aksharanethra_np_e411e388/amazon-athena-querying-s3-data-using-sql-a-hands-on-aws-guide-32i0</guid>
      <description><p>Introduction</p>

<p>When working with large datasets in the cloud, analyzing data often requires setting up databases, servers, or data warehouses. Amazon Athena provides a simpler approach.</p>

<p>Amazon Athena is a serverless interactive query service that allows users to analyze data directly from Amazon S3 using standard SQL.</p>

<p>In this tutorial, we will:</p>

<p>Upload a dataset to Amazon S3<br>
Create a database in Amazon Athena<br>
Create a table for the dataset<br>
Query the data using SQL<br>
View and analyze the query results</p>

<p>For this demonstration, the Stranger Things Dialogue Dataset is used.</p>

<p>What is Amazon Athena?</p>

<p>Amazon Athena is a serverless query service provided by AWS that allows users to run SQL queries directly on data stored in Amazon S3.</p>

<p>Athena does not require:</p>

<p>Dedicated servers<br>
Database installation<br>
Infrastructure management<br>
Database provisioning</p>

<p>You simply point Athena to your data in S3 and use SQL to query it.</p>

<p>Basic Architecture<br>
              User<br>
                |<br>
                ↓<br>
        Amazon Athena<br>
                |<br>
             SQL Query<br>
                |<br>
                ↓<br>
        Amazon S3 Dataset<br>
                |<br>
                ↓<br>
           Query Result</p>

<p>Athena uses the AWS Glue Data Catalog to store information about databases and tables, while the actual data remains in Amazon S3.</p>

<p>Why Use Amazon Athena?</p>

<p>Athena is useful when you need to analyze data stored in S3 without creating and maintaining a traditional database.</p>

<p>Key advantages<br>
Serverless – No servers to manage<br>
SQL-based – Uses familiar SQL syntax<br>
Direct S3 querying – Data can remain in S3<br>
Scalable – Handles large datasets<br>
Pay-per-query – Charges are based primarily on the amount of data scanned<br>
Easy integration – Works with other AWS analytics services<br>
Prerequisites</p>

<p>Before starting, you need:</p>

<p>An AWS account<br>
An S3 bucket<br>
A dataset stored in S3<br>
Access to Amazon Athena<br>
Basic knowledge of SQL</p>

<p>For this demonstration, the S3 bucket used is:</p>

<p>akshara-s3-15-09-2026</p>

<p>The dataset is stored under:</p>

<p>s3://akshara-s3-15-09-2026/stranger-things/</p>

<p>The uploaded files are:</p>

<p>episodes.csv<br>
stranger-things-dialogue-dataset.zip<br>
stranger_things_all_dialogue.csv</p>

<p>Note: In Athena, we will query the CSV file rather than the ZIP file.</p>

<p>Step 1: Upload the Dataset to Amazon S3</p>

<p>The dataset was first downloaded from Kaggle and extracted on an Amazon EC2 instance.</p>

<p>The extracted files were:</p>

<p>episodes.csv<br>
stranger_things_all_dialogue.csv</p>

<p>They were then uploaded to S3 using the AWS CLI:</p>

<p>aws s3 cp . s3://akshara-s3-15-09-2026/stranger-things/ --recursive</p>

<p>To verify the uploaded files:</p>

<p>aws s3 ls s3://akshara-s3-15-09-2026/stranger-things/</p>

<p>The output confirmed that the files were successfully uploaded.</p>

<p>Step 2: Open Amazon Athena<br>
Sign in to the AWS Management Console.<br>
Search for Athena.<br>
Open Amazon Athena.<br>
Select the appropriate AWS Region.</p>

<p>You will be taken to the Athena Query Editor.</p>

<p>Screenshot:<br>
Add screenshot of Amazon Athena Query Editor here.</p>

<p>Step 3: Configure the Query Result Location</p>

<p>Athena needs an S3 location where it can store the results of SQL queries.</p>

<p>In the Athena Query Editor:</p>

<p>Open Settings.<br>
Find Query result location.<br>
Specify an S3 path.</p>

<p>For example:</p>

<p>s3://akshara-s3-15-09-2026/athena-results/<br>
Save the configuration.</p>

<p>The query results generated by Athena will be stored in this location.</p>

<p>Screenshot:<br>
Add screenshot of Athena settings here.</p>

<p>Step 4: Create a Database</p>

<p>We can create a database using SQL.</p>

<p>Run:</p>

<p>CREATE DATABASE stranger_things_db;</p>

<p>After executing the query, select the database:</p>

<p>USE stranger_things_db;</p>

<p>The database provides a logical structure for organizing our tables.</p>

<p>Step 5: Create a Table</p>

<p>Now we need to tell Athena how the CSV file is structured.</p>

<p>Before creating the table, inspect the CSV file and identify its column names.</p>

<p>For example, if the dialogue dataset contains columns such as:</p>

<p>season<br>
episode<br>
character<br>
dialogue</p>

<p>we can create a table using:</p>

<p>CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE stranger_things_dialogue (<br>
    season INT,<br>
    episode STRING,<br>
    character STRING,<br>
    dialogue STRING<br>
)<br>
ROW FORMAT SERDE 'org.apache.hadoop.hive.serde2.OpenCSVSerde'<br>
WITH SERDEPROPERTIES (<br>
    'separatorChar' = ',',<br>
    'quoteChar' = '"'<br>
)<br>
LOCATION 's3://akshara-s3-15-09-2026/stranger-things/'<br>
TBLPROPERTIES ('skip.header.line.count'='1');<br>
Important</p>

<p>The column definitions must match the actual CSV structure.</p>

<p>If your CSV has different column names or data types, modify the CREATE TABLE statement accordingly.</p>

<p>Step 6: Verify the Table</p>

<p>To see the table:</p>

<p>SHOW TABLES;</p>

<p>You should see:</p>

<p>stranger_things_dialogue</p>

<p>You can also inspect the table structure:</p>

<p>DESCRIBE stranger_things_dialogue;</p>

<p>This displays the column names and their data types.</p>

<p>Step 7: Run the First Query</p>

<p>Let's retrieve some records from the dataset.</p>

<p>SELECT *<br>
FROM stranger_things_dialogue<br>
LIMIT 10;</p>

<p>Athena reads the data from S3 and returns the matching records.</p>

<p>Screenshot:<br>
Add screenshot showing the query and results.</p>

<p>Step 8: Count the Number of Dialogue Records</p>

<p>We can use SQL aggregation to determine how many dialogue records exist.</p>

<p>SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_dialogues<br>
FROM stranger_things_dialogue;</p>

<p>This demonstrates how Athena can perform analytical operations directly on S3 data.</p>

<p>Step 9: Find the Most Frequent Characters</p>

<p>We can use GROUP BY to determine which characters appear most frequently.</p>

<p>SELECT character, COUNT(*) AS dialogue_count<br>
FROM stranger_things_dialogue<br>
GROUP BY character<br>
ORDER BY dialogue_count DESC;</p>

<p>This produces a ranking of characters based on the number of dialogue records.</p>

<p>Step 10: Filter Data</p>

<p>Athena supports standard SQL filtering.</p>

<p>For example:</p>

<p>SELECT *<br>
FROM stranger_things_dialogue<br>
WHERE season = 1;</p>

<p>This returns dialogue records belonging to Season 1.</p>

<p>We can also search for a particular word:</p>

<p>SELECT *<br>
FROM stranger_things_dialogue<br>
WHERE LOWER(dialogue) LIKE '%friends%';</p>

<p>This can be useful for text-based analysis.</p>

<p>Step 11: Aggregate Data by Season</p>

<p>We can calculate the number of dialogue records for each season.</p>

<p>SELECT season, COUNT(*) AS dialogue_count<br>
FROM stranger_things_dialogue<br>
GROUP BY season<br>
ORDER BY season;</p>

<p>This allows us to compare dialogue volume across different seasons.</p>

<p>Step 12: Query Results</p>

<p>Athena displays the query results directly in the Query Editor.</p>

<p>The results can also be stored in Amazon S3 using the query result location configured earlier.</p>

<p>This allows the output of Athena queries to be reused by other AWS services or applications.</p>

<p>How Amazon Athena Works</p>

<p>The overall process can be summarized as:</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>    CSV Dataset
         |
         ↓
   Amazon S3
         |
         ↓
  AWS Glue Catalog
         |
         ↓
  Amazon Athena
         |
      SQL Query
         |
         ↓
   Query Results
         |
         ↓
   Amazon S3
</code></pre>

</div>

<p>Athena does not move the original dataset into a traditional database.</p>

<p>Instead, it reads the required data from S3 when a query is executed.</p>

<p>Athena and AWS Glue Data Catalog</p>

<p>Amazon Athena works with the AWS Glue Data Catalog to store metadata about datasets.</p>

<p>Metadata includes information such as:</p>

<p>Database name<br>
Table name<br>
Column names<br>
Data types<br>
S3 data location<br>
File format</p>

<p>The actual dataset continues to reside in S3.</p>

<p>This separation between data and metadata makes Athena suitable for data-lake architectures.</p>

<p>Supported Data Formats</p>

<p>Athena can work with several data formats, including:</p>

<p>CSV<br>
JSON<br>
Apache Parquet<br>
Apache ORC<br>
Avro<br>
Text files</p>

<p>For large-scale analytics, columnar formats such as Parquet can significantly improve query performance because Athena can scan only the required columns.</p>

<p>Advantages of Amazon Athena</p>

<ol>
<li>Serverless</li>
</ol>

<p>There is no infrastructure to provision or maintain.</p>

<ol>
<li>Easy to Use</li>
</ol>

<p>Users can analyze data using familiar SQL queries.</p>

<ol>
<li>Direct S3 Integration</li>
</ol>

<p>Athena can query data stored directly in Amazon S3.</p>

<ol>
<li>Scalable</li>
</ol>

<p>Athena can process datasets ranging from small files to very large data lakes.</p>

<ol>
<li>Cost Efficient</li>
</ol>

<p>There is no need to keep database servers running continuously.</p>

<ol>
<li>Suitable for Data Lakes</li>
</ol>

<p>Athena is particularly useful for analyzing large collections of data stored in S3.</p>

<p>Limitations</p>

<p>Although Athena is powerful, it has some limitations.</p>

<p>Query performance depends on data organization and file format.<br>
Querying large CSV datasets can result in more data being scanned.<br>
Poorly structured data can increase query cost.<br>
Athena is primarily designed for analytics rather than high-frequency transactional workloads.</p>

<p>Using Parquet, partitioning, and efficient data organization can improve performance and reduce costs.</p>

<p>Real-World Applications</p>

<p>Amazon Athena can be used for:</p>

<p>Log analysis<br>
Website analytics<br>
Security analysis<br>
Business intelligence<br>
Data lake analytics<br>
IoT data analysis<br>
Financial data analysis<br>
Application event analysis<br>
Large-scale CSV/JSON data analysis</p>

<p>For example, an organization could store millions of application logs in S3 and use Athena to identify errors without maintaining a dedicated database server.</p>

<p>Amazon Athena vs Traditional Database<br>
Feature Amazon Athena   Traditional Database<br>
Infrastructure  Serverless  Requires servers<br>
Data Storage    Amazon S3   Database storage<br>
Query Language  SQL SQL<br>
Management  Minimal Higher<br>
Scaling Managed by AWS  Usually configured<br>
Best Use    Analytics   Transactional workloads<br>
Data Lake Support   Excellent   Limited<br>
Conclusion</p>

<p>Amazon Athena provides a simple and powerful way to analyze data stored in Amazon S3 using standard SQL.</p>

<p>In this hands-on demonstration, the Stranger Things dialogue dataset was:</p>

<p>Downloaded from Kaggle<br>
Extracted on an EC2 instance<br>
Uploaded to Amazon S3<br>
Registered as an Athena table<br>
Queried using SQL</p>

<p>The main advantage is that we can perform data analysis without creating or managing a database server.</p>

<p>This makes Amazon Athena an important service for serverless analytics and cloud-based data lake architectures.</p>

<p>Key Takeaways<br>
Amazon S3       → Stores the data<br>
AWS Glue        → Stores metadata<br>
Amazon Athena   → Queries the data using SQL<br>
Amazon S3       → Stores query results</p>

<p>Amazon Athena enables serverless SQL-based analytics directly on data stored in Amazon S3.</p>

<p>References<br>
Amazon Athena Documentation<br>
Amazon S3 Documentation<br>
AWS Glue Data Catalog</p>

      <title>Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes: what they actually protect you from</title>
      <dc:creator>Amit Shukla</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Tue, 15 Sep 2026 13:15:41 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/amitshuklabag/kubernetes-readiness-and-liveness-probes-what-they-actually-protect-you-from-197a</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/amitshuklabag/kubernetes-readiness-and-liveness-probes-what-they-actually-protect-you-from-197a</guid>
      <description><p>A pod can be <code>Running</code> and still be useless. The container process is alive, the port is open, and every request that hits it times out anyway, because the database connection pool hasn't finished warming up, or a downstream dependency is unreachable, or the app is stuck in a loop it will never recover from on its own.</p>

<p>Kubernetes has two checks for exactly this, <code>livenessProbe</code> and <code>readinessProbe</code>. They sit next to each other in the same YAML block, take the same shape, and do almost nothing alike.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  What liveness actually does
</h2>

<p>A liveness probe answers one question: is this process still working, or should it be killed and restarted.</p>

<p>If the probe fails enough times in a row, Kubernetes kills the container and starts a fresh one. That's the entire mechanism. It exists for the case where your process is technically running but permanently stuck, a deadlock, a hung thread, a memory leak that's wedged the event loop. Restarting is the only fix, and liveness is what triggers it automatically instead of you finding out from an alert three hours later.</p>

<p>What it does not do: protect you from slow startup, temporary unavailability, or a dependency being down. If your liveness check fails because the database is briefly unreachable, Kubernetes restarts a perfectly healthy process, which does nothing to fix the database and just adds a few seconds of extra downtime while the container comes back up.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  What readiness actually does
</h2>

<p>A readiness probe answers a different question: should this pod currently receive traffic.</p>

<p>If it fails, the pod is pulled out of the Service's list of endpoints. Nothing gets restarted. The container keeps running, Kubernetes just stops routing requests to it until the probe passes again. This is what you want during startup, while dependencies are still initializing, and during temporary trouble, when a downstream service is degraded and you'd rather drain traffic away than serve errors.</p>

<p>Readiness is safe to make strict. Liveness is not.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The mistake that causes the most damage
</h2>

<p>Pointing both probes at the same endpoint, or writing a liveness check that depends on downstream services.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight javascript"><code><span class="c1">// dangerous as a liveness check</span>
<span class="nx">app</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">get</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="dl">'</span><span class="s1">/healthz</span><span class="dl">'</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">async </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">req</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">res</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">=&gt;</span> <span class="p">{</span>
  <span class="k">await</span> <span class="nx">db</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">query</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="dl">'</span><span class="s1">SELECT 1</span><span class="dl">'</span><span class="p">);</span>
  <span class="k">await</span> <span class="nx">redis</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">ping</span><span class="p">();</span>
  <span class="nx">res</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">sendStatus</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">200</span><span class="p">);</span>
<span class="p">});</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>The moment the database is slow or Redis hiccups, every pod running this as its liveness check starts failing and getting restarted, all at once, across the whole deployment. You just turned a downstream blip into a full outage of your own service, and a restart storm on top of it, since the new containers boot up, immediately fail the same check because the dependency is still down, and get killed again.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  What each check should actually look like
</h2>

<p>Liveness should only answer "is the process itself alive," nothing more.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight javascript"><code><span class="c1">// liveness: just prove the event loop is responsive</span>
<span class="nx">app</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">get</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="dl">'</span><span class="s1">/healthz</span><span class="dl">'</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">req</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">res</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">=&gt;</span> <span class="p">{</span>
  <span class="nx">res</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">sendStatus</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">200</span><span class="p">);</span>
<span class="p">});</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Readiness should check the things that actually determine whether this pod can serve a request correctly.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight javascript"><code><span class="c1">// readiness: are the things we depend on actually up</span>
<span class="nx">app</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">get</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="dl">'</span><span class="s1">/ready</span><span class="dl">'</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">async </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">req</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">res</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">=&gt;</span> <span class="p">{</span>
  <span class="k">try</span> <span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="k">await</span> <span class="nx">db</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">query</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="dl">'</span><span class="s1">SELECT 1</span><span class="dl">'</span><span class="p">);</span>
    <span class="nx">res</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">sendStatus</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">200</span><span class="p">);</span>
  <span class="p">}</span> <span class="k">catch</span> <span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="nx">res</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">sendStatus</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">503</span><span class="p">);</span>
  <span class="p">}</span>
<span class="p">});</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>And the pod spec pointing at each:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">livenessProbe</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">httpGet</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">path</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">/healthz</span>
    <span class="na">port</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="m">3000</span>
  <span class="na">initialDelaySeconds</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="m">10</span>
  <span class="na">periodSeconds</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="m">10</span>
  <span class="na">failureThreshold</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="m">3</span>

<span class="na">readinessProbe</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">httpGet</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">path</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">/ready</span>
    <span class="na">port</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="m">3000</span>
  <span class="na">initialDelaySeconds</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="m">5</span>
  <span class="na">periodSeconds</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="m">5</span>
  <span class="na">failureThreshold</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="m">3</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<h2>
  
  
  Tuning that actually matters
</h2>

<p><strong>initialDelaySeconds</strong> on liveness should be longer than your worst-case startup time. If your app can take 20 seconds to boot under load, and liveness starts checking at 10 seconds with a low failure threshold, you'll get restart loops on your slowest starts, which makes the slow start even slower.</p>

<p><strong>failureThreshold and periodSeconds together</strong> define how long a probe has to fail before something happens. Three failures at ten second intervals gives you thirty seconds of grace. Too short and normal jitter triggers unnecessary restarts or traffic pulls. Too long and a genuinely stuck pod keeps eating requests for a while before anyone notices.</p>

<p><strong>Never let liveness depend on anything outside the process.</strong> If it can fail because of a network call, a database, another service, it will eventually cause a restart storm during exactly the incident where you can least afford one.</p>

<p><strong>Readiness can and should depend on those things.</strong> That's the entire point of having it separate. Use it to pull a pod out of rotation the moment it can't correctly serve a request, and let it rejoin automatically the moment it can again, with no restart, no lost in-flight work on the other healthy pods.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Takeaway
</h2>

<p>Liveness restarts a stuck process. Readiness controls whether a pod gets traffic. Keep liveness dumb and self-contained so it only fires when the process itself is actually broken, and keep readiness honest about your real dependencies so Kubernetes can route around trouble instead of amplifying it.</p>

      <title>The Kubernetes Audit Worksheet</title>
      <dc:creator>Kestrion</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Tue, 15 Sep 2026 09:15:18 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/kestrion/the-kubernetes-audit-worksheet-1m30</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/kestrion/the-kubernetes-audit-worksheet-1m30</guid>
      <description><p><em><strong>Do it right from the beginning</strong> ----&gt; Print this, block four hours, and work through it with whoever knows the cluster best. Every command is read-only.</em></p>

<h2>
  
  
  Section 0 — Context (15 min, no terminal)
</h2>

<p>Write down before looking at anything:</p>

<ul>
<li>Business: what runs on this cluster, and what does one hour of downtime cost?</li>
<li>People: who can operate it? Who is the single point of failure?</li>
<li>History: last incident, last upgrade, last restore test (dates, not vibes).</li>
<li>Bill: monthly cloud + observability spend, best guess.</li>
</ul>

<p>You'll compare these answers with reality at the end. The gap is your executive summary.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Section 1 — Inventory (30 min)
</h2>



<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl version                          <span class="c"># in support?</span>
kubectl get nodes <span class="nt">-o</span> wide                <span class="c"># count, versions, ages, pressure</span>
kubectl get ns                           <span class="c"># what exists</span>
kubectl get deploy,sts,ds,cronjob <span class="nt">-A</span>     <span class="c"># workload inventory</span>
helm <span class="nb">ls</span> <span class="nt">-A</span>                               <span class="c"># what Helm thinks is installed</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Record: K8s version and support status, node count/type, workload count, and — critically — <strong>which workloads are NOT represented in any Git repo</strong>. That list is your unreproducible surface.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Section 2 — Deployment path (30 min)
</h2>

<p>Trace one real service from commit to production and write each step down. Then answer:</p>

<ul>
<li>Can anyone deploy by hand to prod? (If yes: who has, recently? Check <code>kubectl rollout history</code>.)</li>
<li>Rollback: exact commands/steps, and when it was last exercised.</li>
<li>Probes and shutdown: for the top 3 services, check readiness probes, <code>preStop</code>, <code>terminationGracePeriodSeconds</code>, rollout strategy, PDBs.
</li>
</ul>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl get deploy &lt;top-service&gt; <span class="nt">-o</span> yaml | <span class="nb">grep</span> <span class="nt">-A5</span> <span class="nt">-E</span> <span class="s2">"readinessProbe|preStop|strategy"</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<h2>
  
  
  Section 3 — Access &amp; secrets (45 min)
</h2>



<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl get clusterrolebindings <span class="nt">-o</span> wide | <span class="nb">grep</span> <span class="nt">-iE</span> <span class="s2">"admin|edit"</span>
kubectl auth can-i get secrets <span class="nt">-n</span> &lt;shared-ns&gt; <span class="nt">--as</span><span class="o">=</span>&lt;a-normal-user&gt;
kubectl get secrets <span class="nt">-A</span> | <span class="nb">wc</span> <span class="nt">-l</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Record: humans with cluster-admin (target: ~0 for daily use), service accounts with broad rights, secret source of truth (ESO/Vault/SOPS vs. hand-created), whether the API server is internet-reachable, and whether any Git repo contains a base64 secret (<code>git grep -i "kind: Secret"</code> across infra repos). Also check <code>kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,clusterpolicies -A</code> — if nothing comes back, there's no admission-time guardrail catching a bad manifest before RBAC and secrets hygiene even get tested.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Section 4 — Cost (45 min)
</h2>

<p>If OpenCost/Kubecost isn't installed, note it as finding #1 and use what you have:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods <span class="nt">-A</span> <span class="nt">--sort-by</span><span class="o">=</span>memory | <span class="nb">head</span> <span class="nt">-30</span>
kubectl describe nodes | <span class="nb">grep</span> <span class="nt">-A8</span> <span class="s2">"Allocated resources"</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Record: requested vs. actually-used CPU/memory ratio (the over-provisioning factor), workloads with <strong>no</strong> requests, count of <code>type: LoadBalancer</code> services, log ingestion GB/day and retention, non-prod running out-of-hours, unattached volumes in the cloud console.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Section 5 — Observability (30 min)
</h2>

<ul>
<li>Where do engineers look first during an incident? (Ask two people separately; different answers = finding.)</li>
<li>Open the alert history for the last 2 weeks: which alerts fired, which led to action? Non-actionable ones are noise debt.</li>
<li>Do golden-signal dashboards exist for the top 3 services?</li>
<li>Certificates: <code>kubectl get certificates -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.status.conditions[]?.status!="True") | .metadata.name'</code> lists cert-manager certs not currently Ready. Is renewal automated AND alerted on failure?</li>
</ul>

<h2>
  
  
  Section 6 — Backup &amp; DR (30 min)
</h2>



<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl get backups <span class="nt">-A</span>          <span class="c"># velero, if present</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Record: what is backed up (cluster state? volumes? databases?), where backups live (outside the blast radius?), last successful backup, <strong>last tested restore</strong>, and estimated time to rebuild everything from Git + backups. If the restore has never been tested, the audit's #1 recommendation writes itself.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Section 7 — Upgrade readiness (20 min)
</h2>



<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubent   <span class="c"># or: pluto detect-all-in-cluster    # deprecated APIs</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Record: versions behind latest, deprecated API usage, add-on versions (ingress, cert-manager, CNI, CSI) and whether anyone owns their lifecycle, existence of a staging cluster or IaC to create one.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Section 8 — Synthesis (45 min)
</h2>

<p>Turn notes into three artifacts:</p>

<ol>
<li>
<strong>Risk map</strong> — every finding rated Impact (1–3) × Likelihood (1–3). Anything 6+ goes on page one. Example: an untested restore is Impact 3 (the business can't recover) × Likelihood 2 (backups exist but nobody's proven they work) = 6.</li>
<li>
<strong>Cost opportunity</strong> — over-provisioning factor + logging retention + orphans, expressed in currency/month.</li>
<li>
<strong>Remediation backlog</strong> — max 10 items, ordered by risk score, each with an effort guess (hours/days/weeks). Default priority when tied: tested restore → rollback → secrets/RBAC → requests cleanup → cert automation → upgrade plan.</li>
</ol>

<p>Finish by re-reading Section 0. The distance between what the team <em>believed</em> and what you <em>found</em> is the story the leadership summary should tell.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  A note on scope
</h2>

<p>This worksheet deliberately excludes application code quality, CI pipeline internals, and cloud account security outside the cluster. Those matter, but mixing them in is how audits become three-week projects nobody finishes. Half a day, cluster-focused, three artifacts out. Done beats comprehensive.</p>

<p>A version of this with 0–100 scoring runs in the browser: the <a href="https://kestrion.dev/scorecard/" rel="noopener noreferrer">free production readiness scorecard</a>.</p>

      <title>How I built a cloud native platform from scratch</title>
      <dc:creator>Jean Silga</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Mon, 14 Sep 2026 13:44:38 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/jeansilga/how-i-built-a-cloud-native-platform-from-scratch-4k9k</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/jeansilga/how-i-built-a-cloud-native-platform-from-scratch-4k9k</guid>
      <description><p>If you read my previous post titled "<a href="https://dev.to/jeansilga/my-journey-to-master-kubernetes-and-cloud-native-196h">My journey to master Kubernetes and Cloud Native</a>", you already know I decided to effectively build a cloud native platform from scratch before taking the CNPE exam. This decision may be rooted in procrastination at its finest: setting an insanely high goal as a precondition to make sure you never reach it…</p>

<p>Bottom line: I decided to build a fully fledged cloud native platform from scratch. Here is how it unfolded.</p>

<p>I started by renting two Virtual Private Servers from Contabo, a German cloud provider. How did I choose the provider? I turned to AI for advice. It gave me five proposals. Contabo was second on the list. I visited their website. The prices were clearly displayed. The proposed services were cleanly explained. The ordering process was straightforward. I settled on them and moved ahead.</p>

<p>I bought two VPS to start with. One with an NVMe drive for the control plane, a second with an SSD for the worker node. Both VPS were up and running, reachable and ready to use within a few minutes. It was a pleasant buying experience.</p>

<p>Then I prepared the control plane to install Kubernetes. I created a dedicated admin account on each node and uploaded my SSH keys so I could log in without typing a password. I went to the official Kubernetes docs and scripted all prerequisites in a Bash file. Then, I wrote an Ansible playbook to run that script on the control plane.</p>

<p>Time for the big moment: <code>kubeadm init</code>.</p>

<p>A few minutes later, I had a Kubernetes control plane staring at me, waiting for a CNI to become ready. I installed Calico and the control plane transitioned to a ready state, waiting for its first worker node.</p>

<p>I raced ahead. I applied a slightly modified version of my init playbook script to the worker node (for instance, no <code>kubectl</code> needed on the worker node). Next, I ran the <code>kubeadm join</code> command. It took a few minutes for the worker node to initialize and join the control plane. And it did.</p>

<p>Now I was looking at a functioning Kubernetes cluster: a control plane and worker node. It felt good. Going from renting the machines to having the Kubernetes cluster up and running took less than an hour.</p>

<p>Before I went on my CNCF Kubernetes certification journey, I wouldn't have had the courage to even try something like that. I surprised myself. The knowledge I gained through that journey, and the confidence it brought, were starting to show in ways I hadn't anticipated. And I was just getting started.</p>

<p>I tore down and rebuilt the cluster many times while perfecting the Bash script I used to init the nodes. For instance, I initially forgot to give a custom hostname to the nodes and only noticed it when the cluster was already up and running. Changing the hostname of a running control plane node can be risky. As I was just getting started, I chose to play it safe. I reinitialized the VM and started over. As I had everything scripted, I was back in business in a matter of minutes.</p>

<p>Remember: my goal was to set up a fully fledged cloud native platform. The Kubernetes cluster was just the first building block, the foundation. Like any foundation, it was a prerequisite for the rest. Now I could install the other building blocks. I installed each one with a Helm chart. Here is the whole platform as it stands today. The rest of this post walks through it, one building block at a time.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fbzw77yzj6u4z8exk5ffh.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fbzw77yzj6u4z8exk5ffh.png" alt="Architecture diagram of the platform, read top to bottom as the traffic flows: a user on the internet reaches an HAProxy proxy node outside the cluster, which forwards the traffic over a private Kube-vip VIP to the Istio gateway inside the Kubernetes cluster, which serves Klatos, the product; below the product, the platform layers it runs on: Longhorn for storage, CloudNativePG for databases, Cert-manager for certificates, OpenBao with External Secrets for secrets, Keycloak for identity, Tekton and Gitea for CI, and Grafana with Prometheus, Loki, Tempo and MinIO for observability; at the bottom of the cluster, ArgoCD pulls the desired state from a GitLab outside it and installs every layer as a Helm chart; underneath, the four rented servers: a proxy node, a control plane and two worker nodes." width="800" height="560"></a></p>

<p><em>Click to open at full size.</em></p>

<p>First stop once Kubernetes was up and running: a GitOps tool. As a Certified Argo Project Associate, my natural choice was ArgoCD. I created the Git repo structure in GitLab to host my Argo Apps manifests, then a deploy token for ArgoCD to authenticate with, then a Kubernetes secret carrying that token so ArgoCD could talk to GitLab on its own. I installed ArgoCD from its Helm chart and wrote the file that is the entry point of every later installation on the cluster: the App of Apps bootstrap. That bootstrap file is the seed. From then on, a Git commit is all it takes for ArgoCD to pick something up and install it in the cluster.</p>

<p>Any Kubernetes setup beyond a hello-world use case needs a storage virtualization tool. The basic <code>hostPath</code> and <code>emptyDir</code> volumes are unsuited to real usage. I settled on Longhorn as a storage orchestrator. Storage redundancy is a prerequisite for any sensible storage virtualization, and so I needed at least a second worker node to pair with the one I had. I kept the control plane out of it. I did not want it involved in storing data.</p>

<p>Overall, I found Longhorn easy to set up, with an attractive benefit/complexity ratio. I also turned on encryption at rest. Longhorn encrypts at the volume level with Linux dm-crypt/LUKS, and I hold the key myself.</p>

<p>For database provisioning, I went with the CloudNativePG operator. It let me create databases for each deployed application with little effort. All I needed to do was create a custom resource with the new database parameters and the operator took care of everything: creating the database, keeping it up, enforcing the desired replica count.</p>

<p>Then came the choice of how to expose services. I settled on using Gateway API over Ingress. Then I picked Istio as a Gateway API provider. I already wanted Istio as a service mesh, mostly for mTLS. Using it as a Gateway API was a bonus. Besides, the setup was straightforward.</p>

<p>The next question to solve was about the IP address the gateway was going to use. Using a static IP of a node was a non-starter for two reasons: first, that would mean the gateway would go down if the node did. And second, I did not want to expose the public IP address of any node of the cluster. I devised a two-step solution. First, I used the Kube-vip utility to set up a private Virtual IP Address that can be moved to any of the cluster nodes dynamically. That way, that VIP stays functional as long as there is a healthy node in the cluster. I assigned that VIP to the gateway. Second, I set up a proxy node outside the cluster to serve as the entry point. That node is powered by HAProxy and is part of the private network of the cluster. It receives the traffic from the internet and then forwards it to the gateway using the VIP.</p>

<p>Next, certificate management. Cert-manager was the obvious choice, and I went with it. My first use was to issue a local Certificate Authority for my internal URLs. The second was more interesting: I connected it to Let's Encrypt, and valid certificates for my public URLs are now generated on the fly. Renewal is also automatic. It took me a few tries, but I got it working.</p>

<p>Next, I needed a vault for secrets. I considered HashiCorp Vault, but eventually settled on OpenBao, an open source fork that appeared when HashiCorp changed its licensing terms. To get the secrets from OpenBao into the Kubernetes cluster, I used the External Secrets Operator.</p>

<p>Up next: Continuous Integration. The CNCF promotes Tekton for this, so I gave it a try. The tool is complex to set up. I struggled with it at the beginning. It took me some time just to understand how many components Tekton has and what each one does. I finally got it up and running. I was glad later that I stuck with it. It was worth the trouble. Now I needed to connect it with a source code repository to test it.</p>

<p>That's when I thought: Tekton runs entirely inside the Kubernetes cluster. It can pull source code from any Git repository and push artifacts to any registry. But what if it pulled the code from inside the cluster and pushed artifacts to a registry inside the cluster too? All CI traffic would stay inside the cluster.</p>

<p>I looked around and Gitea was a good fit: it is a Git server and a container registry in one, it is cloud native and light on resource consumption. Gitea it was.</p>

<p>Then came Identity and Access Management. I needed to settle on how to handle authentication and authorization. That one was easy. I have been working with Keycloak since 2019. No debate.</p>

<p>Observability was on my list too. I wanted to know, at any time, what was going on with anything I deployed, what experience users were having, and to be able to investigate quickly when something went wrong. I went for all three kinds of telemetry data: logs, metrics and traces. I settled on the full Grafana stack and instrumented my apps with OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation to get traces. Prometheus holds the metrics. Loki and Tempo are the backends for logs and traces, with MinIO as the storage behind both.</p>

<p>This is pretty much it. It was quite a ride, instructive and enjoyable. One year ago, I wouldn't have had the courage to take on such a side project. One thing made it possible: the confidence I built through the CNCF certifications.</p>

<p>Once you build such a platform, the natural thing is to find something to deploy on it. As I wrote last time, I had a three-month period at the start of 2026 when I wasn't on a job. To keep track of how I was spending my days, I built an Excel file with a list of daily habits I wanted to hold: physical exercise, meaningful learning, digital restraint, sleep and wake-up hours, journaling, a walk outside, meditation, and so on. I started this file to have an accurate record of how my days were going, instead of relying on gut feeling.</p>

<p>Later, while I was building my cloud native platform, an idea started forming: what if I turned that Excel file into a real app, deployed it on my platform, and shared it with the world? The idea was sensible enough that I decided to give it a try. I had been longing to build an app for some time anyway.</p>

<p>Before, I had been hiding behind two excuses: building was expensive, and I couldn't come up with an idea I thought was worth the trouble. Both excuses were now a thing of the past, for two reasons. AI had significantly lowered the cost of building. And I had more than an idea: I had something tangible, an Excel file I used every day, and knew was worth the trouble.</p>

<p>And one extra motivation, the icing on the cake: a brand-new, fully fledged cloud native platform ready to host the app.</p>

<p>What comes next is a story for another day.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Klatos
</h2>

<p>That Excel file became Klatos: a habit tracker that turns small daily steps into a changed year. It is the first product from Vixoris, and it runs on the platform this post describes.</p>

<p><a href="https://klatos.vixoris.com/?ref=devto" rel="noopener noreferrer">Learn more about Klatos →</a></p>




<p><em>Vixoris — Structures that compound.</em></p>

      <title>Platform Engineering: Der Turbo für Ihre DevOps-Strategie</title>
      <dc:creator>Uhltak Therestismysecret</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Mon, 14 Sep 2026 06:00:40 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/uhltak/platform-engineering-der-turbo-fur-ihre-devops-strategie-2bhl</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/uhltak/platform-engineering-der-turbo-fur-ihre-devops-strategie-2bhl</guid>
      <description><h2>
  
  
  Platform Engineering: Mehr als nur ein Buzzword – Die Zukunft der Softwareentwicklung
</h2>

<p>Die Welt der Softwareentwicklung dreht sich unaufhaltsam weiter. Auf den Hype um DevOps und Cloud-native Architekturen folgt nun der nächste große Trend, der verspricht, die Art und Weise, wie wir Software bauen und betreiben, fundamental zu verändern: <strong>Platform Engineering</strong>. Doch was verbirgt sich hinter diesem Begriff? Ist es nur ein neues Schlagwort für alte Konzepte oder eine echte Revolution, die die „DevOps-Müdigkeit“ endlich beendet? </p>

<p>In diesem Artikel tauchen wir tief in die Welt des Platform Engineering ein. Wir klären, was es ist, wie es sich von DevOps unterscheidet, welche Vorteile es bietet und wie Sie den Grundstein für eine erfolgreiche interne Entwicklerplattform (IDP) in Ihrem Unternehmen legen. Machen Sie sich bereit, denn Platform Engineering ist der Schlüssel zur Steigerung Ihrer Entwicklerproduktivität und zur Beschleunigung Ihrer digitalen Transformation.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Was ist Platform Engineering? Eine klare Definition
</h3>

<p>Im Kern ist Platform Engineering die Disziplin, eine solide, interne Self-Service-Plattform zu entwerfen und zu betreiben, die den gesamten Lebenszyklus der Softwareentwicklung abdeckt. Stellen Sie sich diese Plattform als ein internes Produkt vor, dessen Kunden Ihre eigenen Entwicklerteams sind. Das Hauptziel ist es, die kognitive Last der Entwickler zu reduzieren und die sogenannte <strong>Developer Experience (DevEx)</strong> zu maximieren.</p>

<p>Anstatt dass jedes Team das Rad neu erfinden und sich mit der Komplexität von Cloud-Infrastruktur, Kubernetes-Konfigurationen, CI/CD-Pipelines und Monitoring-Tools herumschlagen muss, bietet die Plattform standardisierte, aber flexible „goldene Pfade“ (Golden Paths). Diese Pfade sind vorab definierte, bewährte Wege, um eine Anwendung zu erstellen, zu testen, bereitzustellen und zu betreiben. Die Entwickler können sich somit wieder voll und ganz auf das konzentrieren, was sie am besten können: hochwertigen Code schreiben und Business-Mehrwert schaffen.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Platform Engineering vs. DevOps: Freund oder Feind?
</h3>

<p>Eine der häufigsten Fragen ist, ob Platform Engineering DevOps ersetzt. Die kurze Antwort lautet: Nein. Platform Engineering ist vielmehr die konsequente Weiterentwicklung und Implementierung der DevOps-Philosophie in großem Stil.</p>

<p>DevOps ist eine Kultur, ein Mindset der Zusammenarbeit zwischen Entwicklung (Dev) und Betrieb (Ops), unterstützt durch eine Reihe von Praktiken und Tools. Das Mantra „You build it, you run it“ hat die Verantwortung direkt in die Entwicklerteams verlagert. Doch dies führte oft zu einer Überlastung.</p>

<h4>
  
  
  Die DevOps-Müdigkeit und die kognitive Last
</h4>

<p>In der Praxis bedeutet „You build it, you run it“ oft auch „You configure it, you secure it, you monitor it, you patch it“. Entwickler sahen sich plötzlich mit einer explodierenden Anzahl an Werkzeugen und Aufgaben konfrontiert: Terraform für die Infrastruktur, Docker für die Containerisierung, Kubernetes für die Orchestrierung, Jenkins oder GitLab für CI/CD, Prometheus und Grafana für das Monitoring, diverse Sicherheitsscanner und vieles mehr. Diese enorme kognitive Last bremst die Produktivität und führt zu Frustration.</p>

<h4>
  
  
  Wie Platform Engineering die Lücke schließt
</h4>

<p>Hier kommt das Platform Engineering ins Spiel. Ein dediziertes <strong>Plattform-Team</strong> übernimmt die Verantwortung für die komplexe zugrundeliegende Infrastruktur und die Toolchain. Es kuratiert und integriert die besten Werkzeuge und stellt sie den Entwicklern über eine einfach zu bedienende <strong>Interne Entwicklerplattform (IDP)</strong> zur Verfügung.</p>

<p>Das DevOps-Mantra entwickelt sich weiter zu: „You build it, you run it – on a platform that makes it simple and secure.“ Die Verantwortung bleibt beim Entwicklerteam, aber die Komplexität wird durch die Plattform abstrahiert.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Die Kernkomponenten einer Internen Entwicklerplattform (IDP)
</h3>

<p>Eine effektive IDP ist mehr als nur eine Sammlung von Skripten. Sie ist ein kohäsives System mit klar definierten Schnittstellen und Funktionen. Zu den wichtigsten Bausteinen gehören:</p>

<h4>
  
  
  Self-Service-Funktionen und Golden Paths
</h4>

<p>Das Herzstück jeder IDP sind die Self-Service-Fähigkeiten. Entwickler sollten in der Lage sein, ohne ein Ticket zu erstellen oder wochenlang auf eine Freigabe zu warten, Standardaufgaben selbstständig durchzuführen. Beispiele hierfür sind:</p>

<ul>
<li>  Ein neues Microservice-Projekt aus einem Template erstellen.</li>
<li>  Eine CI/CD-Pipeline für das neue Projekt provisionieren.</li>
<li>  Eine neue Testumgebung oder eine Datenbank anfordern.</li>
<li>  Ein Feature-Flag aktivieren oder deaktivieren.</li>
</ul>

<p>Diese Aktionen folgen den „Golden Paths“ – vom Plattform-Team vordefinierten, optimierten und sicheren Prozessen.</p>

<h4>
  
  
  Infrastruktur als Code (IaC) als Fundament
</h4>

<p>Die gesamte Plattform und die Ressourcen, die sie verwaltet, basieren auf dem Prinzip der Infrastruktur als Code (IaC). Werkzeuge wie Terraform, Pulumi oder Crossplane werden vom Plattform-Team genutzt, um wiederverwendbare, getestete Module zu erstellen. Entwickler müssen nicht mehr die Details von Cloud-Provider-APIs kennen, sondern können auf diese High-Level-Abstraktionen zurückgreifen.</p>

<h4>
  
  
  Integrierte Toolchain für den gesamten Lebenszyklus
</h4>

<p>Eine IDP integriert Werkzeuge aus allen Phasen der Softwareentwicklung zu einer nahtlosen Kette:</p>

<ul>
<li>  <strong>Code &amp; Build:</strong> Versionskontrolle (z.B. Git), Artefakt-Repositories (z.B. Artifactory).</li>
<li>  <strong>CI/CD:</strong> Continuous Integration &amp; Delivery (z.B. GitLab CI, Jenkins, ArgoCD).</li>
<li>  <strong>Runtime:</strong> Container-Orchestrierung (fast immer Kubernetes), Service Mesh (z.B. Istio).</li>
<li>  <strong>Observability:</strong> Logging (ELK-Stack), Metriken (Prometheus), Tracing (Jaeger).</li>
<li>  <strong>Sicherheit:</strong> Statische Code-Analyse (SAST), Container-Scanning, Policy Enforcement (OPA).</li>
</ul>

<h4>
  
  
  API, CLI und UI: Die Schnittstellen zur Plattform
</h4>

<p>Entwickler interagieren mit der IDP über verschiedene Schnittstellen. Eine gut gestaltete Web-UI (wie sie z.B. von Open-Source-Projekten wie Backstage.io bereitgestellt wird) bietet einen zentralen Anlaufpunkt für Dokumentation, Service-Kataloge und Self-Service-Aktionen. Eine mächtige Kommandozeile (CLI) ermöglicht die Automatisierung und Integration in Skripte, während eine stabile API die programmatische Interaktion mit der Plattform sicherstellt.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Die unschlagbaren Vorteile von Platform Engineering
</h3>

<p>Die Investition in ein Plattform-Team und eine IDP zahlt sich auf vielfältige Weise aus:</p>

<ul>
<li>  <strong>Gesteigerte Entwicklerproduktivität:</strong> Durch die Reduzierung von Reibung und kognitiver Last können sich Entwickler auf die Entwicklung von Features konzentrieren, was direkt den Geschäftserfolg beeinflusst.</li>
<li>  <strong>Schnellere Time-to-Market:</strong> Standardisierte und automatisierte Deployment-Prozesse verkürzen die Zeit von der Idee bis zur Auslieferung an den Kunden drastisch.</li>
<li>  <strong>Verbesserte Standardisierung und Compliance:</strong> Sicherheitsrichtlinien, Best Practices und Compliance-Anforderungen sind direkt in die Plattform und die „Golden Paths“ integriert. Dies reduziert Risiken und vereinfacht Audits.</li>
<li>  <strong>Erhöhte Zuverlässigkeit und Stabilität:</strong> Da die Infrastrukturkomponenten vom Plattform-Team zentral verwaltet, getestet und gehärtet werden, steigt die Gesamtstabilität der betriebenen Anwendungen.</li>
<li>  <strong>Skalierbarkeit der Organisation:</strong> Platform Engineering ermöglicht es, auch bei stark wachsenden Entwicklerzahlen konsistente und effiziente Prozesse beizubehalten.</li>
</ul>

<h3>
  
  
  Fazit: Platform Engineering ist die strategische Antwort auf Komplexität
</h3>

<p>Platform Engineering ist keine vorübergehende Modeerscheinung, sondern eine strategische Notwendigkeit für jedes Unternehmen, das in der heutigen Cloud-nativen Welt erfolgreich sein will. Es ist die logische Konsequenz aus den Erfahrungen, die wir mit DevOps gesammelt haben.</p>

<p>Der Aufbau einer internen Entwicklerplattform ist eine Reise, kein einmaliges Projekt. Der Schlüssel zum Erfolg liegt darin, die Plattform als internes Produkt zu behandeln, kontinuierlich Feedback von den Entwicklern einzuholen und sich auf die Maximierung der Developer Experience zu konzentrieren. Indem Sie die Komplexität der modernen IT-Infrastruktur abstrahieren und Ihren Entwicklern eine stabile, sichere und effiziente Self-Service-Plattform zur Verfügung stellen, schaffen Sie die Grundlage für schnellere Innovation, höhere Qualität und letztlich einen entscheidenden Wettbewerbsvorteil.</p>
