      <title>Instâncias AWS Graviton Instâncias AWS Graviton Arquitetura ARM na Nuvem</title>
      <dc:creator>Kauê Matos</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Sun, 13 Sep 2026 17:04:17 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/ikauedev/instancias-aws-graviton-instancias-aws-graviton-arquitetura-arm-na-nuvem-16d</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/ikauedev/instancias-aws-graviton-instancias-aws-graviton-arquitetura-arm-na-nuvem-16d</guid>
      <description><p>O <strong>AWS Graviton</strong> é uma família de processadores desenvolvidos pela própria AWS, baseados em arquitetura <strong>ARM (64-bit, Arm Neoverse)</strong>, em vez da arquitetura x86 tradicional (Intel/AMD). Lançado inicialmente em 2018, o Graviton se tornou uma das principais estratégias da AWS para oferecer melhor custo-benefício e eficiência energética em instâncias EC2.</p>

<p>Hoje, praticamente todas as famílias de instância "de uso geral" da AWS (M, C, R, T e derivadas) possuem uma variante Graviton, identificada pelo sufixo <strong>g</strong> no nome (ex.: <code>m7g</code>, <code>c7g</code>, <code>r7g</code>, <code>t4g</code>).</p>

<p>Este artigo explica o que é o Graviton, como evoluiu ao longo das gerações, quando vale a pena adotar e quais são os principais cuidados de migração.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  O que é o Graviton
</h2>

<p>Graviton é um <strong>System on Chip (SoC)</strong> projetado pela AWS Annapurna Labs (empresa israelense adquirida pela AWS em 2015), otimizado especificamente para rodar dentro da infraestrutura da própria AWS. Diferente de depender de fornecedores externos (Intel, AMD), a AWS controla o design do chip ponta a ponta — o que permite ajustar a arquitetura ao perfil real de uso dos seus data centers.</p>

<p><strong>Principais vantagens declaradas pela AWS:</strong></p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Melhor custo-benefício</strong> — em geral, 20% a 40% mais barato que instâncias x86 equivalentes.</li>
<li>
<strong>Melhor performance por watt</strong> — até ~60% mais eficiente energeticamente, o que também contribui para metas de sustentabilidade (ESG) das empresas.</li>
<li>
<strong>Performance competitiva ou superior</strong> em cargas de trabalho compatíveis, especialmente as que escalam horizontalmente.</li>
</ul>

<h2>
  
  
  Evolução das gerações
</h2>

<h3>
  
  
  Graviton1 (2018)
</h3>

<p>Primeira geração, lançada com as instâncias <code>a1</code>. Voltada principalmente para cargas escaláveis horizontalmente e workloads que não exigiam alta performance de CPU por núcleo. Adoção limitada, mas serviu como prova de conceito.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Graviton2 (2019/2020)
</h3>

<p>Salto significativo de performance — baseado em núcleos Arm Neoverse N1. Introduziu as variantes <code>g</code> em famílias já conhecidas: <code>m6g</code>, <code>c6g</code>, <code>r6g</code>, <code>t4g</code>. Trouxe suporte a mais casos de uso de produção, com performance comparável a instâncias x86 de geração equivalente.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Graviton3 (2021/2022)
</h3>

<p>Presente em <code>m7g</code>, <code>c7g</code>, <code>r7g</code>, além de instâncias especializadas como <code>c7gn</code> (rede otimizada) e <code>hpc7g</code> (HPC). Trouxe ganhos relevantes em:</p>

<ul>
<li>Performance de ponto flutuante (importante para HPC e ML)</li>
<li>Criptografia acelerada por hardware</li>
<li>Maior largura de banda de memória (DDR5)</li>
</ul>

<h3>
  
  
  Graviton4 (2023/2024)
</h3>

<p>Geração mais recente, presente em instâncias como <code>r8g</code> e <code>m8g</code>. Foco em maior número de núcleos, maior largura de banda de memória e melhorias de segurança, mantendo compatibilidade com o ecossistema ARM já validado nas gerações anteriores.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Famílias disponíveis com Graviton
</h2>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Família x86 equivalente</th>
<th>Variante Graviton</th>
<th>Foco</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>M (uso geral)</td>
<td>m6g, m7g, m8g</td>
<td>Aplicações web, microsserviços</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>C (compute optimized)</td>
<td>c6g, c7g, c7gn</td>
<td>CPU intensiva, rede otimizada</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>R (memory optimized)</td>
<td>r6g, r7g, r8g</td>
<td>Bancos de dados, cache</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>T (burstable)</td>
<td>t4g</td>
<td>Cargas variáveis, dev/test</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>X (memória alta)</td>
<td>x2gd</td>
<td>In-memory databases</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>I (storage optimized)</td>
<td>i4g</td>
<td>NoSQL, alta taxa de I/O</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Hpc</td>
<td>hpc7g</td>
<td>HPC fortemente acoplado</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<h2>
  
  
  Quando vale a pena migrar para Graviton
</h2>

<p><strong>Bons candidatos:</strong></p>

<ul>
<li>Aplicações <strong>stateless</strong> rodando em containers (Docker/Kubernetes) com imagens multi-arquitetura.</li>
<li>Linguagens/runtimes com suporte nativo e maduro a ARM: Java (JVM), Go, Python, Node.js, .NET.</li>
<li>Cargas de trabalho gerenciadas pela própria AWS que já oferecem variante Graviton nativamente: Amazon RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch, EMR.</li>
<li>Workloads horizontalmente escaláveis, onde trocar a arquitetura de um conjunto de instâncias idênticas é simples de validar.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Pontos de atenção antes de migrar:</strong></p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Dependências binárias nativas</strong> (bibliotecas compiladas, extensões C/C++) precisam ter build para ARM64 disponível.</li>
<li>
<strong>Imagens de container</strong> precisam ser multi-arquitetura (<code>docker buildx</code> com suporte a <code>linux/arm64</code>) ou reconstruídas especificamente para ARM.</li>
<li>Softwares proprietários de terceiros (agentes de monitoramento, APM, drivers específicos) precisam ter suporte oficial a ARM confirmado pelo fornecedor.</li>
<li>Testes de performance e carga são recomendados antes de migrar workloads críticas de produção, mesmo com boa compatibilidade declarada.</li>
</ul>

<h2>
  
  
  Estratégia de migração recomendada
</h2>

<ol>
<li>
<strong>Inventariar</strong> as aplicações e suas dependências, verificando compatibilidade com ARM64 (bibliotecas, imagens base de container, agentes de terceiros).</li>
<li>
<strong>Começar pelo menos crítico</strong> — ambientes de desenvolvimento/homologação ou workloads stateless de baixo risco.</li>
<li>
<strong>Rodar testes de carga comparativos</strong> entre a instância x86 atual e a equivalente Graviton, validando performance e custo real.</li>
<li>
<strong>Migrar gradualmente</strong> ambientes de produção, aproveitando Auto Scaling Groups com múltiplos tipos de instância (mixed instance policy) durante a transição.</li>
<li>
<strong>Consolidar o ganho de custo</strong> validado nas etapas anteriores em Savings Plans ou Reserved Instances específicas para a família Graviton escolhida.</li>
</ol>

<h2>
  
  
  Conclusão
</h2>

<p>O Graviton deixou de ser uma opção experimental e se tornou, hoje, a recomendação padrão da AWS para novas cargas de trabalho — quando a stack permite. A combinação de menor custo, menor consumo energético e performance competitiva faz da migração para ARM uma das otimizações de maior impacto disponíveis em uma conta AWS, especialmente quando combinada com outras estratégias de FinOps como Savings Plans e Spot Instances.</p>

<p>Antes de migrar qualquer workload crítica, o caminho mais seguro é sempre: validar compatibilidade, testar performance real e migrar de forma incremental — começando pelos ambientes de menor risco.</p>

      <title>Bypassing the BIOS: Fixing Minikube’s "VT-X/AMD-v Enabled is Mandatory" Error Without a VM</title>
      <dc:creator>Raziq Din</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Sat, 12 Sep 2026 14:54:26 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/raziq_din_bd0274cc2ac748b/bypassing-the-bios-fixing-minikubes-vt-xamd-v-enabled-is-mandatory-error-without-a-vm-4ck8</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/raziq_din_bd0274cc2ac748b/bypassing-the-bios-fixing-minikubes-vt-xamd-v-enabled-is-mandatory-error-without-a-vm-4ck8</guid>
      <description><p>I was interested in touching the surface of Kubernetes ecosystem of some sort , so I decided to touch some minikube to build a service observability and incident respond dashboard. In most cases , you download Minikube, open up your terminal, type minikube start, and wait for the magic to happen. Instead, your console explodes with a massive wall of red text:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>❌ Exiting due to HOST_VIRT_UNAVAILABLE: Failed to start host
💡 Suggestion: Virtualization support is disabled on your computer... consult your systems BIOS manual.

</code></pre>

</div>



<p>The standard advice on the internet tells you to restart your computer, spam the F2 or Delete key like a maniac, enter your motherboard’s terrifying BIOS menu, and hunt for hidden hardware virtualization toggles (VT-x or AMD-v).<br>
&nbsp;<br>
But if you are on a restricted machine, a work laptop ( like mine lol ), or you simply don’t feel like messing with your computer's motherboard firmware just to test some code, there is a much better way. Here is exactly how to resolve the missing VM error by completely changing how Minikube operates.<br>
&nbsp;</p>
<h3>
  
  
  Why Minikube Crashes by Default
</h3>

<p>Minikube was originally engineered back when laptops couldn't run containers easily. To adapt, Minikube defaults to using VirtualBox as a hypervisor. It attempts to build a massive, heavy, virtualized Linux operating system on your machine to act as your Kubernetes server.<br>
If your laptop's CPU doesn't have hardware virtualization explicitly flipped on at the silicon level, VirtualBox panics, drops the connection, and blocks kubectl from finding a cluster node.<br>
&nbsp;</p>
<h3>
  
  
  The Solution: Pivot to Docker Containers (Yes I know its suprising lol)
</h3>

<p>Instead of wasting time trying to make a Virtual Machine work, you can instruct Minikube to ditch VirtualBox entirely. If you have Docker Desktop running on your computer, you can run Kubernetes inside a fast, lightweight container instead. Here is the exact step-by-step resolution path:<br>
&nbsp;</p>
<h4>
  
  
  Step 1: Purge the broken VM footprint
</h4>

<p>First, wipe away the corrupted VirtualBox configuration files holding onto the broken state in your terminal:<br>
&nbsp;<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>minikube delete

</code></pre>

</div>



<p>&nbsp;</p>

<h4>
  
  
  Step 2: Relaunch with the Docker Driver
</h4>

<p>Tell Minikube to bypass hypervisors completely and launch the cluster inside a container system:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>minikube start --driver=docker

</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Minikube switches tactics. It reaches out to your running Docker engine, pulls down the official kicbase image, and spins up a functional Kubernetes control-plane in roughly 10 seconds.<br>
&nbsp;</p>
<h4>
  
  
  Step 3: Run the Verification Check
</h4>

<p>Once the terminal outputs the 🏄 Done! status, you can safely query the cluster using Minikube’s internal tool execution:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>minikube kubectl -- get nodes

</code></pre>

</div>



<p>&nbsp;<br>
Your console will output a clean node marked Ready. The error is gone, your workspace is clean, and you didn't have to restart your laptop once to get it done!<br>
&nbsp;<br>
Example screenshot of the clusters is shown below:</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F9r7yaeejw8dsdr2u35k7.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F9r7yaeejw8dsdr2u35k7.png" alt="Minikube Cluster Success" width="800" height="98"></a></p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p>You will also be able to see your Minikube is running actively in your docker desktop , as Minikube has successfully uses docker as it's main container to run its cluster</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2For6ks1mu40xuh82xy95e.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2For6ks1mu40xuh82xy95e.png" alt="Docker Desktop Success" width="793" height="47"></a></p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Key Takeaways
</h3>

<ul>
<li><p><strong>Containers Over Hypervisors:</strong><br>
Switching to <code>--driver=docker</code> treats your Kubernetes node as a standard container rather than a full virtual machine. This bypasses host-level hypervisor checks and avoids BIOS lockouts entirely.<br>
&nbsp;</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Lower Resource Footprint:</strong><br>
VM drivers like VirtualBox or Hyper-V allocate fixed slabs of RAM and CPU overhead up front. The Docker driver shares the host Docker engine's daemon, spinning up nodes faster with lower idle memory consumption.</p></li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<br>
Thank you for the read , let me know in the comments of your thoughts and happy experimenting with cloud native tools!</p>

</description>

      <title>Azure Functions to Container Apps, One Endpoint at a Time</title>
      <dc:creator>Martin Oehlert</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 11 Sep 2026 06:06:01 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/martin_oehlert/azure-functions-to-container-apps-one-endpoint-at-a-time-2e1</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/martin_oehlert/azure-functions-to-container-apps-one-endpoint-at-a-time-2e1</guid>
      <description><p>You have <code>/api/orders/*</code> running on a Dapr-enabled Container App in staging and <code>/api/reports/*</code> nowhere near ready, and Azure Front Door will move production traffic for you either way. The two ways are different objects and you cannot get one from the other: a <strong>route</strong> maps a set of path patterns to exactly one <strong>origin group</strong>, while a <strong>weight</strong> splits traffic between origins <em>inside</em> a single origin group. Take the route and the cutover happens one path at a time, reverting by deleting a pattern. Take the weight and both runtimes have to serve every path on that route, and the ratio you typed does nothing at all until you change a load balancing setting almost nobody mentions. The four phases below are the order those two levers go in, and what each one costs you when it goes wrong.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Phase 1: deploy alongside and route nothing
</h2>

<p>The running scenario for the rest of this article: an order API on <code>api.contoso.com</code>, fronted by a Front Door Standard profile, with a single route whose patterns are <code>['/*']</code> pointing at a Function App origin. Everything is on that one route today. <code>/api/orders/*</code> moves to the Container App first, <code>/api/reports/*</code> moves last.</p>

<p>Phase 1 adds two things and changes nothing else. The Container App gets deployed and registered in the Front Door profile as an origin in its own origin group. No route points at that group yet, so it serves zero production requests, and the only claim phase 1 makes is that Front Door can reach it and gets a 200 back from a probe.</p>

<p>The <code>/*</code> route stays exactly where it is, for the whole migration. It is the <strong>catch-all</strong>: the fallback for every endpoint you have not moved yet, and the thing that catches a path back when you revert one. Front Door has no implicit default, and a request matching no route errors out with one of two status codes depending on which doc you read, so do not build anything that inspects the code.</p>

<p>Everything here is Front Door Standard/Premium, resource type <code>Microsoft.Cdn/profiles</code>. Front Door classic (<code>Microsoft.Network/frontDoors</code>) <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/frontdoor/tier-migration" rel="noopener noreferrer">retires on 2027-03-31</a>: no new profiles, no new domain onboarding, no new managed certificates. If your existing profile is classic, the migration in front of you is a different one from this article's.</p>

<p>The ordering decision worth making now is which path goes last, and <code>/api/reports/*</code> is last here for a reason that is not "reports matter less". Front Door's <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/frontdoor/how-to-configure-origin#origin-response-timeout" rel="noopener noreferrer">origin response timeout</a> is 16 to 240 seconds, and "this timeout value is applied to all endpoints in the Azure Front Door profile". A long-running report path cannot be given a longer timeout than the order path next to it. Whichever endpoint has the widest latency spread sets the number for the whole profile, so you move it when you have the most information.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  The probe is the first thing that breaks
</h3>

<p>Front Door's health probe has a rule that reads as a detail and behaves as an outage: <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/frontdoor/health-probes" rel="noopener noreferrer">only 200 OK counts as healthy</a>. Not 204, not 301. Put a Function App whose <code>/healthz</code> returns 204, which plenty do on purpose, in an origin group next to a container that returns 200, and you have manufactured an outage in the component you added to prevent one.</p>

<p>The second rule contradicts the first place you would look: the probe path is case sensitive, while route path patterns are case insensitive, to the point that Front Door rejects <code>/FOO</code> and <code>/foo</code> as duplicates in the same field.</p>

<p>The Container Apps side is quieter and worse. With ingress enabled and no probes defined, Container Apps <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-apps/health-probes#default-configuration" rel="noopener noreferrer">adds defaults</a> that are TCP checks against the ingress target port, and a TCP probe passes as long as something is bound to it. A process that is listening and broken, whose database connection died on startup or whose configuration failed to bind, passes every default probe it gets: false green, at the exact moment you are looking for evidence that the new runtime works.</p>

<p>On top of startup, readiness and liveness, a Dapr-enabled app adds a fourth opinion: the sidecar's <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-apps/dapr-overview" rel="noopener noreferrer">own app health probe</a> (<code>dapr.appHealth</code>, with its own path, interval, timeout and threshold), which decides whether the sidecar considers your app up. That is a separate question from whether the platform considers the replica up, and from whether Front Door considers the origin healthy.</p>

<p>Collapse it onto one answer: one HTTP health endpoint returning exactly 200, the same path with the same casing on both origins, and explicit probes replacing the TCP defaults so the container's readiness reflects the check Front Door is making:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">probes</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">type</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">Readiness</span>
    <span class="na">httpGet</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="na">path</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">/healthz</span>      <span class="c1"># same string, same casing, as the Front Door probePath</span>
      <span class="na">port</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="m">8080</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Then have the Function App serve <code>/healthz</code> at 200 too, before you point a single probe at it, and check which verb you are probing with while you are there. New profiles default to <code>HEAD</code>, which is the right choice for load, and a <code>MapGet</code> answers it with 405 while an <code>[HttpTrigger(..., "get")]</code> answers it with 404. Either add the verb on both origins or set <code>probeRequestType: 'GET'</code>, because the rule at the top of this aside does not care why the response was not a 200.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Phase 2: send the new endpoints and nothing else
</h2>

<p>Phase 2 is the first config that carries traffic, and it is two resources: an origin group for the orders path, and a route pointing at it. Everything else in the profile is untouched.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>resource ordersOriginGroup 'Microsoft.Cdn/profiles/originGroups@2021-06-01' = {
  name: 'orders-origin-group'
  parent: frontDoorProfile
  properties: {
    loadBalancingSettings: {
      sampleSize: 4
      successfulSamplesRequired: 3
      // Load-bearing, and it does nothing in phase 2. Leave it at the default 0 and the
      // weights you set in phase 3 are ignored entirely. See "Your 90/10 split is a
      // 100/0 split" below.
      additionalLatencyInMilliseconds: 500
    }
    healthProbeSettings: {
      probePath: '/healthz'          // case sensitive, unlike patternsToMatch
      probeRequestType: 'HEAD'
      probeProtocol: 'Https'
      probeIntervalInSeconds: 30     // set it; the documented default varies by source
    }
  }
}

resource ordersRoute 'Microsoft.Cdn/profiles/afdEndpoints/routes@2021-06-01' = {
  name: 'orders-route'
  parent: frontDoorEndpoint
  dependsOn: [ ordersOrigin ]   // the origin group must not be empty when the route is created
  properties: {
    originGroup: { id: ordersOriginGroup.id }
    supportedProtocols: [ 'Https' ]
    // Both patterns, deliberately. The wildcard rules do not settle whether
    // '/api/orders/*' also matches a bare '/api/orders', and POST /api/orders is the
    // create-order call. Listing both is correct either way and costs nothing.
    patternsToMatch: [ '/api/orders', '/api/orders/*' ]
    forwardingProtocol: 'HttpsOnly'
    linkToDefaultDomain: 'Enabled'
    httpsRedirect: 'Enabled'
  }
}
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>The <code>/*</code> route from phase 1 is still deployed and still points at the Function App, and nothing about this new route mentions it. That omission is why the strangler fig shape works in Front Door: there is no priority field on a route and declaration order is irrelevant. Front Door "always matches to the most-specific request by evaluating the left-hand side properties: protocol, domain, and path, in that order", with the frontend host matched exactly and the path matched against exact patterns first, wildcard patterns second. <code>/api/orders/12345</code> hits <code>orders-route</code> and <code>/api/reports/monthly</code> falls through to the catch-all, and you did not order anything to make that happen.</p>

<p>The wildcard syntax has three rules and they are all about the end of the string: <code>*</code> is valid only as the last character, with nothing after it, preceded by <code>/</code>. A pattern with no wildcard is an exact match, and so is a pattern ending in <code>/</code>, which is the one that catches people:</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fc0u0lsulj3k69xknr3gs.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fc0u0lsulj3k69xknr3gs.png" alt="How Front Door matches a request against route patterns, most specific first" width="800" height="240"></a></p>

<p>The CLI equivalent, if your Front Door is not in Bicep yet:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>az afd route create <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--resource-group</span> rg-orders <span class="nt">--profile-name</span> afd-orders <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--endpoint-name</span> orders-endpoint <span class="nt">--route-name</span> orders-route <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--origin-group</span> orders-origin-group <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--patterns-to-match</span> <span class="s2">"[/api/orders,/api/orders/*]"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--supported-protocols</span> <span class="s2">"[Https]"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--forwarding-protocol</span> HttpsOnly <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--https-redirect</span> Enabled <span class="nt">--link-to-default-domain</span> Enabled
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>There is no <code>--cache-configuration</code> flag on that command, and its absence is the setting: omitting it leaves caching off for the route. A migrating order API wants it off badly enough that phase 3 spends an aside on what happens if you forget.</p>

<p>Doing this one path at a time has a ceiling, and it is far away: a Standard profile allows 100 routes and 100 origin groups (Premium doubles both), 100 path patterns per route, and a composite limit of 5000 routes per profile counted as domains multiplied by paths. An API with thirty endpoints is not close to any of those.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  A route is a switch, not a dial
</h3>

<p>Read the route above as a percentage control and you will misread the whole migration. A route maps its patterns to exactly one origin group and 100% of matching requests go there. There is no weight, ratio or percentage anywhere in a route's properties, and no partial state between "the Function App serves <code>/api/orders</code>" and "the Container App serves it".</p>

<p>The percentage lever lives one level down: <strong>origin weights</strong>, integers from 1 to 1000, on the origins inside a single origin group. That is a different object with different behaviour, and the two do not compose the way most migration write-ups imply. You cannot put 10% of <code>/api/orders/*</code> on the Container App by editing a route, because what the route selects is the group, not the origin. Which leaves a design fork that decides the rest of your migration:</p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Two origin groups plus two routes.</strong> Per-path cutover, no percentage available. You revert by removing a pattern from <code>patternsToMatch</code>, and the catch-all route re-catches the path. Blast radius is one path pattern.</li>
<li>
<strong>One origin group plus two origins.</strong> Percentage rollout by weight, reverted by disabling the new origin. The cost is that both origins are eligible for every path on that route, so the Function App and the Container App each have to serve the whole pattern set.</li>
</ul>

<p>Phase 2 is the first shape, deliberately: a path you have never sent a request to is the cheapest thing in the world to move, and the revert is one line of config. Phase 3 is the second shape, where the weights come out and turn out not to work at their defaults.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  The host header decides which app answers
</h3>

<p>Both origins need one property that has no obvious symptom when it is missing, because Front Door is documented to fill it in for you: "If you use Azure Resource Manager templates or another method without explicitly setting this field, Front Door sends the incoming host name as the value for the host header." Omit <code>originHostHeader</code> in Bicep and the Container App receives <code>Host: api.contoso.com</code>.</p>

<p>That breaks on both sides, and harder on the new one. App Service and Functions want the host header to match the backend domain unless the custom domain is bound to the app. Container Apps goes further: the environment's ingress proxy routes traffic to the correct app, revision and replica <em>based on host headers</em>, so a wrong header is not a mismatched certificate, it is the environment being unable to work out which of your apps you meant. Set it explicitly on each origin, and keep both lines next to each other so the asymmetry is obvious in review:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>originHostHeader: 'orders-api.orangeplant-77e5875b.westeurope.azurecontainerapps.io'  // Container App
originHostHeader: 'orders-func.azurewebsites.net'                                     // Function App
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>The same property decides which app answers a probe, so an unset host header can turn phase 1's green probe into a phase 2 outage without either config changing in between.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Both runtimes on one Service Bus topic
</h2>

<p>Phase 2 moved an HTTP path. The order topic is the first Azure resource both runtimes hold at once, and it is where a migration stops being a routing exercise. Three files decide whether that goes well, and the same string appears in all three.</p>

<p>The Dapr component on the Container App:<br>
</p>

<p>The Function App, unchanged, still deployed, still consuming:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight csharp"><code><span class="p">[</span><span class="nf">Function</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">nameof</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">ProcessOrder</span><span class="p">))]</span>

<p>And the scale rule on the Container App, which is the file people forget is part of the same decision:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>scale: {
  minReplicas: 0
  maxReplicas: 10
  rules: [ { name: 'orders-topic', custom: {
    type: 'azure-servicebus'
    identity: 'system'

      topicName: 'orders'

<p><code>orders-fn</code> three times, in three different formats, validated by nothing.</p>

<p>That shared string buys you the second row of a two-row decision, and that decision is the whole coexistence story. A <strong>subscription</strong> on a Service Bus topic "resembles a virtual queue that receives copies of the messages that are sent to the topic", and every subscription gets <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/service-bus-messaging/service-bus-queues-topics-subscriptions#topics-and-subscriptions" rel="noopener noreferrer">its own copy</a> of every published message. The number of subscriptions is the number of times each order gets processed.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F5lnkepjmna9dx46mhf4i.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F5lnkepjmna9dx46mhf4i.png" alt="Two Service Bus topic topologies: separate subscriptions process every order twice, one shared subscription makes the runtimes competing consumers" width="800" height="187"></a></p>

<p>The second row is a supported configuration rather than a hack. Subscriptions "support the same patterns described earlier in this section regarding queues: competing consumer, temporal decoupling, load leveling, and load balancing." Dapr already does it to itself: replicas sharing an <code>app-id</code> get each message delivered to <a href="https://docs.dapr.io/developing-applications/building-blocks/pubsub/pubsub-overview/" rel="noopener noreferrer">"only one instance of that application"</a>, so adding the Function widens an existing race rather than starting a new one. Which runtime wins any given race is not something you get to know, so do not write a handler whose correctness depends on which side processed order 41.</p>

<p>One default changes load rather than behaviour, so nothing will page you about it. Dapr's <code>maxConcurrentHandlers</code> defaults to <code>0</code>, meaning unlimited; the Functions host's <code>maxConcurrentCalls</code> defaults to <code>16</code>. Point both runtimes at the same downstream database and the new side applies materially more concurrent pressure than the side it replaces, on a number nobody typed.</p>

<p>Sessions are the one mismatch here that fails loudly, at component init. Session properties belong to the <strong>subscription metadata</strong> rather than the component metadata (<code>requireSessions</code>, default <code>false</code>; <code>maxConcurrentSessions</code>, default 8), and the Functions equivalent is <code>IsSessionsEnabled</code>. Point a default Dapr subscriber at a session-enabled subscription the Function has been draining for two years and the component source returns <code>subscription %s already exists but session requirement doesn't match</code>, with nothing in the portal mentioning sessions. If you enable sessions on the Dapr side, check the concurrency number too: 8 against the Functions host's 2000 is a drop of two and a half orders of magnitude.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  consumerID is the subscription name, and it defaults to your app ID
</h3>

<p>The Dapr reference page describes <code>consumerID</code> as a grouping label. Verbatim: "Consumer ID (consumer tag) organizes one or more consumers into a group. Consumers with the same consumer ID work as one virtual consumer ... If the <code>consumerID</code> is not provided, the Dapr runtime set it to the Dapr application ID (<code>appID</code>) value."</p>

<p>Read that as a label and you will leave it unset. The component source says what the page does not, which is that the value is a name of a real Azure entity:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight go"><code><span class="c">// pubsub/azure/servicebus/topics/servicebus.go</span>
<span class="n">r</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">rErr</span> <span class="o">:=</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">client</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">GetClient</span><span class="p">()</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">NewReceiverForSubscription</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">req</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">Topic</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">metadata</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">ConsumerID</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="no">nil</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="o">...</span>
<span class="n">err</span> <span class="o">:=</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">client</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">EnsureSubscription</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">subscribeCtx</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">metadata</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">ConsumerID</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">req</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">Topic</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">opts</span><span class="p">)</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p><code>ConsumerID</code> goes straight into <code>NewReceiverForSubscription</code> and <code>EnsureSubscription</code> as the subscription argument. The consumer ID <strong>is</strong> the Service Bus subscription name. That mapping comes from <a href="https://github.com/dapr/components-contrib/blob/main/pubsub/azure/servicebus/topics/servicebus.go" rel="noopener noreferrer">components-contrib</a>, not from the reference page, so cite the source if you have to defend it in review.</p>

<p>Follow the default through the migration and you get a specific outcome. Deploy the Container App with app ID <code>orders-api</code> and no <code>consumerID</code>, and Dapr creates a Service Bus subscription literally named <code>orders-api</code> and consumes from it. Nothing about <code>orders-fn</code> changes. The Function keeps working perfectly. You are now in the first row of that table: every order processed twice, by two runtimes, with no error raised anywhere, and the only visible symptom is downstream. Duplicate confirmation emails, doubled inventory decrements, two rows where you expected one.</p>

<p>The second half of the pairing is the scale rule. <code>subscriptionName</code> in the KEDA <code>azure-servicebus</code> rule is the entity KEDA polls to decide how many replicas you need. <code>consumerID</code> is the entity Dapr drains. Both are naming the same kind of thing, so if the two strings differ, KEDA is measuring a backlog that the app it is scaling will never touch. The failure is quiet in the direction that matters: with <code>minReplicas: 0</code>, KEDA watches a subscription that stays empty, keeps the app at zero replicas, and the subscription that is actually filling up has no consumer at all. Nothing validates the pair, in either resource.</p>

<p>Entity management is the third thing the component does that a migration does not want it doing. <code>disableEntityManagement</code> defaults to <code>"false"</code>, meaning create-if-missing. The source shows what "automatically" costs: the component builds a second, administrative client, and <code>EnsureSubscription</code> calls <code>EnsureTopic</code> and then <code>GetSubscription</code> before deciding whether to create anything. A failed <code>GetSubscription</code> is an error rather than a shrug:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight go"><code><span class="n">res</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">err</span> <span class="o">:=</span> <span class="n">c</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">adminClient</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">GetSubscription</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">ctx</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">topic</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">subscription</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="no">nil</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="k">if</span> <span class="n">err</span> <span class="o">!=</span> <span class="no">nil</span> <span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="no">false</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">fmt</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">Errorf</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"could not get subscription %s: %w"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">subscription</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">err</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p><code>GetSubscription</code> is a management-plane call. A Container App whose managed identity holds only <code>Azure Service Bus Data Receiver</code> has no path to the management plane, so on that reading subscription setup fails at init while the identity holds every right it needs to actually receive messages. The permission that looks correct on a least-privilege review is the one that stops the sidecar from starting. That chain is read off the source rather than watched, so treat the exact failure text as unconfirmed until you have the sidecar log in front of you.</p>

<p>One related waste of time. Four fields in the component reference (<code>lockDurationInSec</code>, <code>maxDeliveryCount</code>, <code>defaultMessageTimeToLiveInSec</code>, <code>autoDeleteOnIdleInSec</code>) each carry the qualifier "Used during subscription creation only", and the source confirms there is no update path. In a migration you are always pointing at a subscription that already exists, so all four are inert: setting <code>maxDeliveryCount</code> in your component YAML changes nothing about how many times a message is delivered. Set it on the Service Bus entity.</p>

<p><strong>What to do instead</strong>, and it is the file at the top of this section. Set <code>consumerID</code> explicitly to the Function's existing subscription name. Set <code>disableEntityManagement: "true"</code>. Pre-create the topic and the subscription in the Function App's existing bicep, which already owns them. Make the KEDA <code>subscriptionName</code> the same literal, and if your infrastructure is in Bicep, make it the same variable so the compiler enforces what neither service does. Then grep for that string before you deploy: it should appear in the component, the trigger attribute, and the scale rule, and nowhere else.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  The envelope goes one way cleanly and one way silently
</h3>

<p>Dapr "uses the CloudEvents 1.0 specification as its message format" and wraps outgoing messages <a href="https://docs.dapr.io/developing-applications/building-blocks/pubsub/pubsub-cloudevents/" rel="noopener noreferrer">automatically</a>. Publish an order from the Container App and this is what lands on the topic:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight json"><code><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"topic"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"orders"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"pubsubname"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"orders-pubsub"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"data"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nl">"orderId"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"order-123"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nl">"customerId"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"cust-42"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="nl">"total"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="mf">89.50</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">},</span><span class="w">

<p>Your order is in there, one level down, under <code>data</code>. Going the other way costs nothing: the Function publishes a bare order body with the SDK, and "the subscribing Dapr process still wraps these raw messages in a CloudEvent before delivering them to the subscribing application", so the handler receives an envelope whose <code>data</code> is the body the Function sent. The direction that breaks is the one you will deploy second, where the Function's existing trigger binds to <code>Order</code>:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight csharp"><code><span class="p">[</span><span class="nf">Function</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">nameof</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">ProcessOrder</span><span class="p">))]</span>
<span class="k">public</span> <span class="n">Task</span> <span class="nf">ProcessOrder</span><span class="p">(</span>
    <span class="p">[</span><span class="nf">ServiceBusTrigger</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"orders"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="s">"orders-fn"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">Connection</span> <span class="p">=</span> <span class="s">"ServiceBus"</span><span class="p">)]</span> <span class="n">Order</span> <span class="n">order</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="c1">// order.OrderId    is null</span>
    <span class="c1">// order.CustomerId is null</span>
    <span class="c1">// order.Total      is 0</span>
    <span class="n">logger</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">LogInformation</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"Processing order {OrderId}"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">order</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">OrderId</span><span class="p">);</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">Task</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">CompletedTask</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>The binding deserializes the message body, and the body is now the envelope. <code>topic</code> and <code>specversion</code> are not properties of <code>Order</code>, and <code>OrderId</code> is not a property of a CloudEvent, so every field lands on its default, with no exception thrown, because the JSON is valid and the type is populated with nothing. The message completes, the delivery count never increments, nothing dead-letters, and <code>DeadletteredMessages</code> stays flat while every order silently evaporates.</p>

<p>There is a documented switch that makes the problem go away, and it costs more than it looks. Setting <code>rawPayload: "true"</code> on publish stops Dapr wrapping the message, but the same page states that disabling CloudEvents <a href="https://docs.dapr.io/developing-applications/building-blocks/pubsub/pubsub-raw/" rel="noopener noreferrer">"disables support for tracing, event deduplication per messageId, content-type metadata, and any other features built using the CloudEvent schema"</a>, and the subscribe side is then "always base64 encoded with content type <code>application/octet-stream</code>". Trading tracing away is a bad deal in a migration whose whole argument is that a single trace spans both sides of it.</p>

<p>So teach the Function about the envelope rather than teaching Dapr to stop producing it. The shim is a record and one property access:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight csharp"><code><span class="k">public</span> <span class="k">sealed</span> <span class="k">record</span> <span class="nc">CloudEvent</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="n">T</span><span class="p">&gt;(</span>
    <span class="p">[</span><span class="n">property</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nf">JsonPropertyName</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"data"</span><span class="p">)]</span> <span class="n">T</span> <span class="n">Data</span><span class="p">,</span>
    <span class="p">[</span><span class="n">property</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nf">JsonPropertyName</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"id"</span><span class="p">)]</span> <span class="kt">string</span> <span class="n">Id</span><span class="p">,</span>
    <span class="p">[</span><span class="n">property</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nf">JsonPropertyName</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"type"</span><span class="p">)]</span> <span class="kt">string</span> <span class="n">Type</span><span class="p">,</span>
    <span class="p">[</span><span class="n">property</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nf">JsonPropertyName</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"traceparent"</span><span class="p">)]</span> <span class="kt">string</span><span class="p">?</span> <span class="n">TraceParent</span><span class="p">);</span>

<span class="p">[</span><span class="nf">Function</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">nameof</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">ProcessOrder</span><span class="p">))]</span>
<span class="k">public</span> <span class="n">Task</span> <span class="nf">ProcessOrder</span><span class="p">(</span>
    <span class="p">[</span><span class="nf">ServiceBusTrigger</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"orders"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="s">"orders-fn"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">Connection</span> <span class="p">=</span> <span class="s">"ServiceBus"</span><span class="p">)]</span> <span class="n">CloudEvent</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="n">Order</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="n">message</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="kt">var</span> <span class="n">order</span> <span class="p">=</span> <span class="n">message</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">Data</span><span class="p">;</span>
    <span class="n">logger</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">LogInformation</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s">"Processing order {OrderId} from event {EventId}"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">order</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">OrderId</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">message</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">Id</span><span class="p">);</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">Task</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">CompletedTask</span><span class="p">;</span>
